body.p: Favorable reconsideration of this application as presently amended and in light of the following discussion is respectfully requested.
Claims 1-20 are pending. Claims 1, 13 and 17 are amended by the present response. Support for the amendments to the claims is found, at least, on page 1, lines 8-14. Thus, no new matter is added.
In the outstanding Office Action, Claims 1-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
With regard to the rejection of Claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 101, Applicant

respectfully traverses this rejection. In particular, it is believed the USPTO's "2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance," issued January 7, 2019 (hereinafter "2019 Revised Guidance")' supports a finding of eligibility in the present case.

According to the 2019 Revised Guidance, the "abstract idea" judicial exception is limited to three categories: (a) mathematical concepts; (b) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (c) mental processes.2
In the present case, the claimed application cannot reasonably be asserted as fitting into any of these three categories.
The outstanding Office Action asserts that the claims are directed to an abstract idea because the claims are directed to a "mental process." Applicant respectfully traverses this assertion.

Applicant respectfully traverses this assertion and submits that a person could not reasonably perform the claimed features mentally. Applicant respectfully submits that the claimed features are simply too complicated to be performed by a human mind as would be universally understood by those of ordinary skill in the art.

For example, Example 37 in the provided SME examples notes that "The claim does not recite any of the judicial exceptions enumerated in the 2019 PEG. For instance, the claim does not recite a mental process because the claim, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, does not cover performance in the mind but for the recitation of generic computer components."

The Action appears to improperly boil the claim down to into individual parts and then review the parts individually to determine whether there is an abstract idea recited therein. This is an improper mischaracterization of the claim. In particular, when the claim is considered as a whole, it is clear that the features of the claim cannot be performed in the human mind.
Specifically, the claimed features require extremely complicated action by a processor that cannot reasonably be performed entirely by a human.

Furthermore, it should be noted that independent Claim 1 has been amended to further emphasize that the claimed features are not practicably performed in the human mind. Specifically, Claim 1 now specifies that the 3D structural image stems from acquisition by a medical imaging device. Thus, Claim 1 now recites a method of processing of an image that stems from real-world physical measurements by a real-world physical technical means (medical imagery), where the processing consists in voxelizing the image according to the claimed method. Thereby, it is abundantly clear that the features of the claim are not directed to the abstract idea of a mental process.

body.p: However, even if it was considered that the claims include an abstract idea, the claims include a practical application. Specifically, with regard to element (}, the claims clearly integrate the features the Action considered to be abstract into a practical application.
The PEG guidance states that:

In the context of revised Step 2A, the following exemplary considerations are indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) may have integrated the exception into a practical application:
- an additional element reflects an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field;
- an additional element that applies or uses a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition;
- an additional element implements a judicial exception with, or uses a judicial exception in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim;
- an additional element effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; and

- an additional element applies or uses the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment, such that the claim as a whole is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
Specifically, the PEG guidance further states that:

It is critical that examiners consider the SVG {EMBED HERE} 0.3271.13 when evaluating whether thejudicial exception is meaningfully limited by practical application of the exception. Some elements may be enough on their own to meaningfully limit an exception, but other times it is the combination of elements that provide the practical application. When evaluating whether an element (or combination of elements) integrates an exception into a practical application, examiners should give careful consideration to both the element and how it is used or arranged in the claim as a whole. Because revised Step 2A does not evaluate whether an additional element is well-understood, routine, conventional activity, examiners are reminded that a claim that includes conventional elements may still integrate an exception into a practical application, thereby satisfying the subject matter eligibility requirement of Section 101. (emphasis added).
When considering the claim as a whole it is not reasonable to assert that that claims do
not include a practical application.
The Action asserts that "the claim limitations that are not indicative of integration into a
practical application." However, this is not correct and is not supported by the evidence.
Furthermore, the Action has provided no rationale to support this conclusion. The claims
clearly provide a significant improvement to the operation of the computer. In fact, Applicant
submits that independent Claim 1 does not pertain to the improvement of generic imaging but
specifically voxelizing a 3D structural medical image. This is a highly complicated computer
based operation that is a critical improvement to medical imaging generation.
In this context, Applicant respectfully submits that the computer-implemented

processing of a technical input (i.e. data, here an image, that stems from real-world physical measurements by a real-world physical technical means), is a technical practical purpose. As such, the claimed method is inherently computer-based and intrinsically a computer- implemented improvement to the technology.
Thus, for at least this additional reason the claims are eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 and the rejection should be withdrawn.
Furthermore, even if the claims were considered to be abstract (which they are not as is noted above), the claims include significantly more under step 2B of the Alice test.
In particular, the pending claims represent techniques that are not well-understood, routine or conventional.
In fact, the claims are directed to a significant improvement. Similarly to the McRO case, the claimed application is able to provide features that were not possible in the past.
In particular, the invention improves the operation of generation of a voxelized 3D
structural medical image. This is clearly s technical improvement to the technology and is in no way conventional.

At least on this basis, it is respectfully submitted that the pending claim features do not represent a well-understood, routine, and conventional technique. As discussed with regard to Enfish, the claims represent an improvement that is more than a computer implementation of "fundamental practices long prevalent in their fields" and therefore are not subject to Alice's holdings that such claims are still considered abstract.

In view of the above remarks, Applicant respectfully submits that the pending claims define patent eligible subject matter and requests that the Office reconsider and withdraw the §101 rejection of the claims.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of Claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. §101 be withdrawn.

For the reasons discussed above, no further issues are believed to be outstanding in the present application and the present application is believed to be in condition for formal allowance. Therefore, a Notice of Allowance for Claims 1-20 is earnestly solicited.

Consequently, in light of the above discussion and in view of the present amendment, the present application is in condition for formal allowance and an early and favorable action to that effect is requested.
